Forgers
FOR-jurz
n. plural (fabricators of falsehood; those who manufacture lies, here applied theologically)
Old French forgier, from Latin fabricare, to make, construct — applied figuratively to those who construct falsehoods as a smith forges metal.

Biblical Definition

But ye are forgers of lies, ye are all physicians of no value.

Job levels this charge against his three friends, whose theology was not random error but constructed, built falsehood — a coherent, confidently argued system insisting that Job's suffering must prove hidden sin. Forgers implies deliberate fabrication, not innocent confusion: the friends have taken a true principle, that sin brings consequence, and hammered it into a false universal, that all suffering proves sin, applying their forged theology to Job's wounds like physicians of no value, worsening the patient while claiming to diagnose him. The verse stands as a permanent warning that confident, systematic, even sincerely-held theology can still be forged falsehood if it is built to explain away a mystery rather than to submit to it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from FORGE: to fabricate or construct falsely; applied to counterfeit documents, and figuratively to constructed lies.

expand to see more

FORGE, v.t. To fabricate; to make falsely, as a document or coin; figuratively, to invent or contrive a falsehood.

FORGERS, n. plural. Those who construct or fabricate falsehood.

Job's charge against his three friends' confident theology.

Implies deliberate, systematic construction, not innocent error.

Paired with physicians of no value, a failed diagnosis worsening the patient.

Key Scripture

Job 13:4 — "But ye are forgers of lies, ye are all physicians of no value."

Modern Corruption

Confident theological systems can themselves become forgers of lies when a true principle is hammered into a false universal, exactly the error Job's friends committed by insisting suffering always proves hidden sin.

expand to see more

It is tempting to assume sincerity and theological confidence are sufficient guards against error. Job's friends were sincere, systematic, and entirely wrong, their forged theology constructed to explain away a mystery — innocent suffering — that Scripture elsewhere refuses to resolve so simply.

The corrective is epistemic humility before mystery: the book of Job as a whole never fully explains Job's suffering to Job himself, and the friends' forged certainty, however coherent, is condemned precisely for refusing the kind of restraint the text itself models.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tophley sheqer, literally plasterers or smearers of falsehood, an image of applying a false coating over a wound rather than healing it — vivid and fitting beside the physicians of no value that follows.
